title: Does Whole-Body Cryotherapy Work?
summary: Josh and Chuck examine whole-body cryotherapy, the trend of standing in a cold chamber filled with vaporized liquid nitrogen gas. They trace its history from Japanese doctor Yamauchi in the 1970s treating rheumatoid arthritis, through Soviet athletes, and back to cold water immersion and polar bear plunges, including Professor Sugarman. They explain the sports-medicine rationale for ice baths and why it conflicts with muscle recovery and inflammation. They cover costs, unregulated spas, the Henderson, Nevada death of a worker who asphyxiated, Nevada's suggested guidelines, Justin Gatlin's frostbite after entering wet, and studies (2013, 2014 placebo "magic soap" bath, 2015 review) finding little evidence beyond reduced inflammation. The episode closes with a listener voicemail from Emily about a broken nose and injections.

segments.title: Opening banter and wart-freezing tangent
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck open with a Squarespace ad read, introduce the topic of whole-body cryotherapy, and digress into personal stories about freezing warts and skin tags and a movie tangent.

segments.title: History: Yamauchi, Soviet athletes, and cold plunges
segments.summary: Japanese doctor Yamauchi is credited with first using cryotherapy for rheumatoid arthritis in the 1970s. The treatment spread to Europe, the Soviet bloc, and then the US. The hosts describe the older tradition of cold water plunges, including Finnish ice swimming and Professor Sugarman in New York.

segments.title: Cold water immersion in sports medicine
segments.summary: Cold water immersion entered sports medicine, with the idea that it draws fluid out of exercised muscles. The hosts argue this conflicts with vasoconstriction. They cite research on cycling ability, Joseph Costello on inflammation as part of recovery, and a Washington Post article.

segments.title: Costs and availability of cryotherapy
segments.summary: Cryotherapy sessions at spas cost about forty to fifty dollars, or less with monthly memberships. The hosts discuss the cold chamber and how gas, unlike liquid, lets people tolerate extreme cold for two to three minutes.

segments.title: Science of nitrogen gas exposure and marketing claims
segments.summary: Liquid nitrogen gasifies at around negative 256 F. Gas tolerance is explained by its lower heat conductivity compared with liquid. Spas claim benefits such as destroying toxins, boosting metabolism, boosting immunity and slowing aging, which the hosts treat skeptically.

segments.title: Henderson, Nevada death and safety guidelines
segments.summary: A worker at Rejuvenice in Henderson, Nevada was found dead in a cryotherapy chamber. The cause was asphyxiation from nitrogen, not freezing. Nevada issued suggested guidelines and recommended warning signs and waivers.

segments.title: Justin Gatlin frostbite, scientific studies, and placebo effect
segments.summary: Sprinter Justin Gatlin got frostbite after entering wet socks and shoes. A lawsuit involved wet gloves. The hosts review studies: a 2014 Australian study with a placebo 'magic soap' bath, a 2013 University of New Hampshire icing study, and a 2012 study showing no difference from ice baths. They conclude the benefits are likely placebo, beyond some inflammation reduction.

segments.title: Closing reflections on cryotherapy
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck reflect that people keep seeking fountain-of-youth cures, while remaining open to undiscovered effects, and note the practice is unpleasant.

segments.title: Listener mail: Emily on broken nose injections
segments.summary: Listener Emily, a Harvard freshman, describes getting five injections into her nose after a broken nose and disputes the hosts' claim that gum injections are the worst.
